text:
A CPU branch predictor tries to guess the outcome of conditional branches before the processor actually knows the result. Because modern CPUs execute instructions in parallel and out of order, they cannot wait for every branch to be resolved; instead, they speculatively execute the path they think is most likely. The predictor maintains a small table of entries, often indexed by the branch address, that stores hints about whether that branch has historically been taken or not taken.

The simplest predictors use a one-bit counter per branch: if the branch was taken last time, the predictor guesses taken; if not taken, it guesses not taken. More advanced designs use two-bit saturating counters, which make the prediction more stable by requiring the branch to be taken or not taken twice before flipping the guess. Even more sophisticated predictors, such as tournament or perceptron-based predictors, combine multiple sources of information—like global branch history, target addresses, and recent patterns—to improve accuracy on complex or correlated branches.

When the actual branch result is finally computed, the CPU compares it with the prediction. If the prediction was correct, the speculative work is simply committed. If it was wrong, the processor must flush the incorrectly executed instructions, redirect the instruction stream to the correct path, and update the predictor’s state so future guesses are better. This feedback loop is why branch prediction
